entries.q: **Issue** When AI is given a command, and fails to find a path, or is otherwise given subsequent commands before the previous are accomplished, server performanc tanks. If AI fails to perform an action once, and fails a second time, it is MUCH better to just undeploy the AI and deploy a new AI, than it is to try give the same AI subsequent commands; even if the newly deployed AI will be deploying to the same area, will be given the same sort of command, and also fails to find a path. The dev team should consider determining what about a failed move-to command causes subsequent move-to commands

entries.q: ## Describe the Issue Clearly I found two major bugs in these functions: mod.MoveObjectOverTime and mod.SetObjectTransformOverTime. ## Steps to Reproduce 1️⃣ Scale & Rotation Corruption when Using Scaled Objects If a spatial object’s scale has been modified even slightly in the Godot editor, calling either of these functions immediately resets the visual scale back to 1, completely breaks its rotation, and starts moving the object with the collision size still based on the original scale. This makes it impossible to animate any object that has been scaled. 2️⃣ Position Drift During Long-Distan
a: I too worked from day one of release to animate objects combined into structures. If the altered scale was the issue, I built structures using only objects with scale set to 1 and tried animating them. While this solved the rotation data corruption problem, another coordinate offset issue caused them to fall apart after moving.

The same applies when calculating based on the relative coordinates between objects. If you absolutely need to move a structure composed of combined objects, you can currently achieve discrete, jerky motion by using functions like MoveObject that do not employ interpolation animation.

Brute forced translation for a group of objects based solely on the root object `ObjId` as a workaround. Basically an iterative method over the `ObjId` heirarchy moving them all at the same time. Rotation will be a different beast but that's up next after I clean this up
entries.tt: Two Critical Bugs in MoveObjectOverTime and SetObjectTransformOverTime (Scale & Position Drift)

entries.q: Can you explain how you intend to store spatial data in the strings file or even the script? a: So the runtime is parsing your strings.json file and making it available at runtime which I am then making use of to load in each key and value. At runtime the code decodes the custom hexadecimal representation to get the original compressed data. Then decompression runs to get the binary data. Finally the binary data is then parsed into a set of objects representing each spatial object that is to be spawned with Spawn object. This whole thing will only work with purely visual assets. My tool that runs initially will only put assets into the binary blob that don't have any additional propertie
I see. So it's essentially a custom encoding of spatial objects that you can decode, parse, and runtime spawn when the game starts. Correct?
But everything else is working properly. Once I fix that I'll make a new thread for it

And I've done it in a way that is more compressible than standard floats would be. (By using a fixed point int effectively) Basically I'm dividing the world up into a grid (16x16 currently) then within that each object can be positioned with 65535 steps giving a minimum accuracy of 0.00024414435034714 which should be like 0.244mm.

It is supposed to return a reference identity `Squad` to be used for comparisons, but it returns a unique one every single time it is called, even for the same `Player` or `teamNumber`/`squadNumber`. It is fundamentally broken. I assume it was overlooked as part of a last-minute API addition because the union type `mod.Object` does not even include `Squad`.

I think it should have been fixed in 1.1.2.0. But what I am seeing is that `mod.Equals` might not support the `player` type, so that's its own issue. Then we'd have to just make `mod.Equals` work with more data types.

a: Grouping by Nodes. If you have objects that are grouped as "children" in the hierarchy tree under another object or node and change their XYZ coordinates, that will be however meters from the "parent" object origin point, instead of the world origin point. If you change the XYZ coordinates of the "parent" object/node, it will move the whole group.

entries.q: Hey everyone! I’ve been working on an [`Events` module](<link> to make event handling in Portal significantly cleaner and more modular. **Why use it?** In BF6 Portal, you must export and define an event handler as Global code, once per event type, which leads to some ugly code if more than one of your systems needs to subscribe to the same event. This module solves that by exposing a central subscription API. This lets you subscribe to the same event from multiple different files or scopes, without them conflicting, and provides a way to unsubscribe dynamically. It handles all the boilerplate
a: New update now allow for this: ```ts import { Events } from 'bf6-portal-utils/events'; // Creates a listener that will call the complete function when the hunter kills the target function createBounty(hunter: mod.Player, target: mod.Player, complete: () => void) { const unsubscribe = Events.OnPlayerEarnedKill.subscribe((player, victim) => { if (mod.Equals(player, hunter) && mod.Equals(victim, target)) { unsubscribe(); // Stop listening complete(); // Bounty done } }); } ```

entries.q: Does anyone know about the execution order of event handlers? I'm wondering if it's possible to create a function that is guaranteed to execute at the very end of each in-game tick. (I'm using TypeScript)
a: I wouldn't really really rely on execution order of most, if not all, events. Also, there is no such thing as "at the end of the tick". You can pretend that the start of a new tick is the end of the last tick, since there is no parallel JS execution, so the next `OngoingGlobal` will definitely fire after the _synchronous_ code for previously fired events are complete.

And _synchronous_ is an important distinction there. The macrotask queue will fill with event triggers from the game, and the microtask queue of the next event loop will fill up with any async code you have. The micro task queue is processed (up to an environment-defined max depth, which we do not know) and then an item from the macro task is processed.

entries.q: ```markdown When monitoring a relatively idle server, you might notice a curious pattern: the script lag starts around `33ms`, stays there for a minute or two, and then smoothly drifts down to `0ms`. **This is not a bug!** It is a normal phenomenon caused by the game engine's internal **Task Scheduler** and how it aligns with the server's tick rate. Here is what is happening under the hood: - **Tick Quantization (The 33ms Jump):** A 30Hz server processes exactly one tick every `~33.33ms`. The engine only evaluates `setTimeout` (technically `mod.Wait`) wake-up calls _on these tick boundaries_.
a: So using this module, you can scale your compute based off of the server health getters it exposes

actually the better way to explain why it's not feasible to see below 33 milliseconds on that metric is because only the server knows when the JavaScript process is done for that tick. The best we can do with our code is to know the time between ticks. That explanation above is more for the timeout (`mod.Wait`) lag, which actually does give some insights into SFT when it finally converges

entries.q: It's nice to know is that the server has a 50 ms safety cap on what can happen during a single tick. Overloading per tick event with a lot of work will just results in the server silently discarding the JavaScript context once it reaches that long. So no crashes, just prolonged reduced server tick rates

entries.q: The `receiver` parameter can actually be left undefined which means the UI enemy will be for the entire server. Also specifically with `SolidUI` you shouldn't need to manually update anything as any `Accessor` or store passed as a property will automatically update the UI element when the underlying `Accessor` is updated.
a: New `bf6-portal-utils` `v9.2.0` released with new `SolidUI` feature: **deferred tick coalescing**. Previously, all UI component properties that were reactively bound would be updated (underlying `mod` call to update the UI widget) as soon as the underlying signal (the value it is listening to) changed, via a microtask during the same tick. Now, you can pass an option to for each and any `SolidUI` managed component with `deferredTicks`, which will coalesce all updates due to signal changes that each respective property is listening to, and only actually update the UI widget property after the n

entries.q: I found my answers. Here is a summary: Global modifiers in Portal apply to bots or soldiers on a global basis. Per-player modifiers in blocks/script replace the global modifiers on a per-person basis, not to scale. In other words, if you set the global health of players to 500%, and then you set a single person's health by script to 50%, their health is 50% of normal, not 50% of 500%. In other words, their health is 50 not 250. Additionally, soldiers versus bots in the global portal modifiers behaves similarly. a: Like said, getting a fixed camera will always give you back a non-null JavaScript variable, but it is opaque. The variable is only valid if the camera is valid. I think for all intents and purposes you can consider any object with a position with z, y and Z being between -0.01 and 0.01 as invalid unless you know you specifically put it there.

What triggers the flight event is an area trigger being tripped N number of times by players. When the trigger occurs, I have a variable that tells all the other spawns to stop spawning 1 second in advance of the dedicated pilot spawner. This seems to help reduce the chances of getting an 'invalid' spawn. Then, I spawn the dedicated pilot using a dedicate pilot spawner. I set the dedicated pilot's name to the same sequence of normal bot names, so that if the validity che
a: What shows in the server browser is based on a lottery system. Your server is unlikely to win the lottery. It is a dumb system that does a disservice to showing what is good about portal, because winning the lottery is random and once you are in the list, it is hard to fall out of the list. This causes a lot of garbage servers to continue to be highlighted and keeps others from having the opportunity. The bar to fall off the list is too low, and it does not take into account ping to highlight better options. <link>
They let us host servers and then make sure that NO ONE can see it. What The Actual

Once a server is on the list, people play it. If people want to play it, because it appears popular, they may host a new version if the available version's ping is higher than they like. They have a chance of winning the lottery. And now there is a second one. This is another problem that causes servers that win the lottery to compound into highlighting the same experience more and more. It is really dumb. You join some of them, and they are just default everything, default spawns, default broken (bad spawns and everything, I mean) custom map spatial file, no script, no spawn protection or any

Some people speculate that low rank players are more likely to win the recommended server lottery so that they are more likely to have engagement with other humans in the server they host. If that is true, it exacerbates the issue because they don't know what is good and what is clickbait 0 effort garbage; because as a new player they are more likely to search of 'bots' or 'level up' or all that stuff that is actually broken or misleading clickbait garbage at this point. They are too new to know what is clickbait.

So for example, on your event handles such as `OnPlayerJoinGame(player: mod.Player) {}`, you get a `mod.Player` argument, but if you do `player.myCustomVariable = 5` that won't do anything, since the `player` you receive as an argument is just a reference to the game engine

entries.q: are maps in typescript not dynamic?
a: So to avoid having to track when the transition started/ended, which you'll need to do for lerping. I would integrate it over multiple steps, you can keep the lerp, just make `t` static, and you can change it to change the speed at which it interpolates.

Try this out: ```ts if (this.scoretext) { if (this.currectscore != this.targetscore) { this.currectscore = lerp(this.currectscore, this.targetscore, 0.1) } mod.SetUITextLabel(this.scoretext, mod.Message(Math.floor(this.currectscore))) } ```
You can increase or decrese the `0.1` to speed up or slow down the transition

In both createSignal(...).emit and emitSignal, you call signalStore.emit(signal, args). Because SignalStore.emit is declared with a rest parameter (...args), that call wraps your payload in another array. So a listener wired up with connect((player) => ...) actually receives [player]. When your handler passes that through to modlib.getPlayerId, the mod API ends up with an array instead of a mod.Player, which will either throw or just return the wrong value.

For 3 hours i was debugging my code trying to find out why an object was stuck at 0, 0, 0. turns out the spacial i pushed never actually updated on server side ( there was never an id for the object ). The current flow for updating anything portal side is as follows (works 100% of the time ) - Delete Script & Strings - Save editor with a change to the title or description - Remove Spatial - Save editor with a change to the title or description - Attach spatial ( if utilized ) - Save editor with a change to the title or description - Add S

entries.q: I ran into the scaling issue with rotation using `mod.SetObjectTransformOverTime` and translation with `mod.MoveObjectOverTime`. Moving a scaled object along one axis with `mod.MoveObjectOverTime` also seems to introduce rotation by the same amount. It's also not possible to move groups of objects using a common parent object; only the parent object moves. This makes it impossible to animate an "assembly" of objects
a: I too worked from day one of release to animate objects combined into structures. If the altered scale was the issue, I built structures using only objects with scale set to 1 and tried animating them. While this solved the rotation data corruption problem, another coordinate offset issue caused them to fall apart after moving.

The same applies when calculating based on the relative coordinates between objects. If you absolutely need to move a structure composed of combined objects, you can currently achieve discrete, jerky motion by using functions like MoveObject that do not employ interpolation animation.

Brute forced translation for a group of objects based solely on the root object `ObjId` as a workaround. Basically an iterative method over the `ObjId` heirarchy moving them all at the same time. Rotation will be a different beast but that's up next after I clean this up

But as written, this script is compatible only with FX that repeat/loop.
You need to create a other script.

entries.q: I found an issue where a WorldIcon becomes completely transparent if its color values are all set to 0. ⸻ Steps to reproduce: 1. In Godot, place a WorldIcon and assign an ObjId (leave all other properties at default). 2. In either a script or the visual editor, call EnableWorldIconImage to enable that icon. 3. In-game, nothing appears at the location where the WorldIcon should be. ⸻ If I change the color property in Godot to any non-zero value, or call SetWorldIconColor in script, the icon displays correctly. However, since this behavior isn’t documented, I’ve seen many beginners give up think
a: I think what is going on is that the WorldIcons are being applied to the HUD with something like Additive Blending, which means you will not be able to show black, and any color you give it will look "dimmer" and "whiter". If you try "almost black" (1,1,1) it will be barely visible as well.

1,1,1 is white, and 0,0,0 is black If you enable text and apply a text with script you can get black text if you set the color for the worldIcon to black. Both the text and the icon will follow the same color

Also incase people didn't know you can use \`\`\`ts for typescript syntax highlighting in code blocks in discord

The way the block editor exports code isn't typically how you'd write it when using TS directly. They do it as such because it's one of the only logical ways to handle the modular nature of it. With TS scripts, you organize it in a way that makes sense to you. You wouldn't necessarily split out the conditions in to their own functions (unless it makes sense ofc) Also if you are working directly with code, please please please try and avoid the use of any 😄

Because for your code above if I completed it in its entirety, it might look like this ```ts export function OnPlayerJoinGame(eventPlayer: mod.Player): void { handleGracePeriod(eventPlayer); } async function handleGracePeriod(player: mod.Player) { if(mod.Equals(player, mod.GetTeam(1)) { mod.EnablePlayerDeploy(player, false); await mod.Wait(20); mod.EnablePlayerDeploy(mod.EventPlayer(),true) } } ```

a: Javascript doesn't support them so TS doesn't. I went looking when I was making my workaround vector class

entries.q: Since launch, calling one of these functions will cause the other's value to be reset to the default. This means it is currently **impossible** to have a capture point with a custom capturing time and a custom neutralization time. ## Steps to reproduce ```ts export async function OnGameModeStarted(): Promise<void> { let exampleCapturePoint = mod.GetCapturePoint(0); // This behaves as expected. // The capture point's capturing time is set to 5 seconds, and it's neutralization time is left untouched. mod.SetCapturePointCapturingTime(exampleCapturePoint, 5); await mod.Wait(10); // Wait 10 seconds
a: That actually makes sense of why my neutralization time didn't work, it was set second in my code. There's a few bugs like this where they seem to be caching old values and applying them instead of the new ones, I encountered the same thing with certain VO functions.
Thanks for noting that. Makes sense. And deeply frustrating. Thought there may have been a fix by now but alas not. As you say Andy - this is critical.
Yup, really messes up the flow of modes. Hoping this get fixed asap!

Okay - solved the issue now I know what it is (this is a temporary workaround). Thanks for the heads up - tried everything but now I know what the problem is it was much easier! ```typescript let captureTime = 5; let neutralisationTime = 2; On capturing export async function OnCapturePointCapturing( eventCapturePoint: mod.CapturePoint ) { mod.SetCapturePointCapturingTime(eventCapturePoint, captureTime); } On Captured export async function OnCapturePointCaptured( eventCapturePoint: mod.CapturePoint ) { mod.SetCapturePointNeutralizationTime(eventCapturePoint, neutralisationTime); } ```

entries.q: ### Feature Description Disable the TypeScript `noImplicitAny` rule. With the update to v1.1.1.0, the rules editor no longer allows `` or ``. This enforces all TS type checker rules that the Portal has configured, one of which is `noImplicitAny` (<link> Typically, this is a good thing. However, it prevents the use of raw JS files, although they may be valid, to be used as a script. This means using a bundler such as esbuild or rollup is off the table. In turn, this prevents us from dividing our script into multiple files, easily sharing and using user-made libraries specif
a: you can use a fake any to get around the js thing

I'm aware. In fact, you can use just regular old `any` as that's explicit rather than implicit. The issue is that bundlers will spit out JS, which, by definition, is valid TS, but with type annotations removed. This was previously accepted via `` but is no longer accepted. That means that we can't (easily) use bundlers thereby disabling libraries, etc. (which the bundler all throws in a single file, as required by Portal). I could add `: any` to each var/param in the resultant JS, but that's a huge pain and not easily done with a bundler.
Disabling also means we can fit less code, since we are forced to specify types in a lot of places. I'd say bringing back (or even allowing to upload JS directly) would be the best solution.

Figured it out FINALLY why SetTeam didn't work.. * you can only do SetTeam on an AI spawned by the AISpawner. Backfill and Static ones don't work. * you can only do SetTeam on yourself if you set a team that you are not currently on, otherwise you get an invalid team input exception. * you can only do SetTeam on players which are not deployed, so you have to undeploy them first.

entries.q: Hey all — I’ve hit a major limitation while building custom Portal modes that prevents a ton of asymmetric ideas from working properly. ## The Problem Right now, the server player count is tied directly to team sizes. Example: 16v16 = a 32-player server. Because of that: > **When the lobby is full, players cannot be swapped between teams.** This breaks any mode where teams are supposed to change dynamically. **Real examples I’ve encountered:** - My **Snipers vs Runners** mode: I want to shuffle who becomes sniper next round — impossible if the lobby is full. - A **Zombies / Infected** mode: 32
a: Yeah exactly. Its an unfortunate bottleneck. Someone did mention to try using FFA and I think this could actually work. BUT it would be much better if there was an official solution to this
When you add teams you have to select the number of players for each team can have. And that ups the total player on the server, and as more people would join it would just autofill all spots.
Nice. Okay I appreciate this. I will try it out and see if it works. Either way it would be nice if there were some server config options to deal with this type of thing.

entries.q: Hey everyone! I’ve put together a **BF6 Portal Mod Template** to make building and managing Portal Mods much easier. The main thing it solves: **you can organize your project however you want**, and it still produces a **single merged file** that the Portal web interface can load. This is especially useful for people who prefer **script over blocks**. It also includes: - 🚀 Ready-to-use TypeScript setup - 🔧 Auto-merge + watch mode for instant rebuilds - 🧩 Produces no errors in VS Code - 📁 Simple `npm install` → start modding - 📝 Updated README with setup instructions If you want an easy, ready-

entries.q: After a lot of typescript debugging, I can confirm that `GetSquad` is literally not even implemented correctly in Portal. It is supposed to return a reference identity `Squad` to be used for comparisons, but it returns a unique one every single time it is called, even for the same `Player` or `teamNumber`/`squadNumber`. It is fundamentally broken. I assume it was overlooked as part of a last-minute API addition because the union type `mod.Object` does not even include `Squad`.
a: I think it should have been fixed in 1.1.2.0. But what I am seeing is that `mod.Equals` might not support the `player` type, so that's its own issue. Could you try and play an SFX on a specific squad (while your local player is on that squad) and seeing if it works? From what I'm seeing, that should. Then we'd have to just make `mod.Equals` work with more data types.

It's just a bit strage that even in `1.1.2.0`, the `mod.Squad` type is not in the union of `mod.Object`. See <link> So you cannot even do `mod.GetObjId(mod.GetSquad(eventPlayer))` and because of that, I don't think you can do `mod.GetSquad(eventPlayer) == mod.GetSquad(eventPlayer)`. Nonetheless, I will try right now.

**Okay, I can confirm that playing music to a squad, works.** So it seems you just can't compare the return value of `GetSquad` whether you pass in a player or a team number and squad number. And you also can't get the object ID of a Squad because trying to do that will fall. Effectively, the issue is that: - the union type `mod.Object` needs to include `mod.Squad` - `mod.Equals` needs to work with `mod.Squad` - `mod.GetObjId` needs to work with `mod.Squad`

a: A `class` is just a fancy way to organize some code that's part of the same "use" or "system", especially if that system is stateful. It's a particularly good way to organize code so it can be a reusable module that isn't coupled to any specific experience. So the logger is its own thing that has its own state and functions and properties, and the UI creation functions are its own thing, and the bounty hunter mechanics are its own thing, and the free-for-all spawns are its own thing, etc.

The `OnPlayerDamaged` also provides some `WeaponUnlock` value, with absolutely zero documentation or indication on what that is. If somehow it referenced the weapon used to deal the damage (then it's a terrible name), then you can apply additional damage to the victim based on the damage actually dealt in the event. The only other issue with this is that it wouldn't show up as natural damage dealt in the on-screen indicators for either player. Would be pretty jank.

This is where I'm at with the project at the moment. I have a high resolution mesh that covers 99% of the map, and another smaller chunk with a much higher resolution of detail shown in the screenshots. As I said I'll make a post detailing everything later on, but I'll go over the jist of how it works for anyone interested. Basically I create a grid of raycasts, save their results to the log file, then parse through that with a custom python script that converts the points into a .obj file. Some of the shortcomings right now are how long the mesh takes to generate and the memory limits I'm hitting. There may be workarounds for these but I'm not sure.

entries.q: Hey everyone, Handling sounds in Battlefield Portal can be area of friction as there are nuances that come with managing sound objects, durations, and spawn overheads, and the native API is strictly functional, a bit scattered, and under-documented. I wrote a `Sounds` class to abstract that away and give us a cleaner, object-oriented way to manage audio. **Highlights:** * **Object-Oriented Control:** `play2D` and `play3D` methods return a `PlayedSound` object. This gives you a direct handle to `stop()` that specific sound instance whenever you want—perfect for looping effects or player-state a
a: New version out now that supports changing sound amplitude for sounds, even while they are playing, and custom fades. You can fade from the current amplitude to any amplitude, with custom durations and and steps. Naturally, there are breaking changes, but they are minimal for the one-shot style usage. This version is an overhaul under the hood, so there is no resource optimizations (previously there was resource pooling and reuse) since 3D sound assets cannot be moved and are fixed to where they are spawned. Another overhaul is planned to introduce: - asset optimizations for 2D sounds - stoppi
entries.tt: Sounds Module (Object-Oriented with spawned resource management)

entries.q: Summary: Community servers have always been a core pillar of Battlefield. To keep Portal attractive and sustainable long-term, server hosts need Full XP support combined with significantly expanded server settings, similar to earlier Battlefield titles. Current Issues: • Full XP is highly restricted in Portal • Many important server settings are missing or unnecessarily linked together • Community servers lack flexibility to adapt to different playstyles • Hardcore and classic Battlefield experiences are heavily limited Requested Features: • Full XP for verified Portal servers (and more modes
a: When you play, you play for fun — but you still want to level up your weapons. That’s part of the game. And the black day is when you don’t get any experience points while playing — even when you’re playing custom modes — because experience points are part of the game. Strictly speaking, the black day started with matchmaking. The golden age was custom servers, custom rules, custom modes — all with full XP. So the black day came with Battlefield 1 and Battlefield V.

entries.q: Hey everyone! I just released a stable version of the [`SolidUI` module](<link> that brings modern, reactive UI development to BF6 Portal. **Why use it?** If you've written complex UI in Portal, you know the pain of manually updating widgets. You have to track state, find the right widget, and call the setters every time something changes. `SolidUI` eliminates that entirely. It’s inspired by SolidJS, meaning it uses **Signals** to track state. When you update a signal, the specific UI properties bound to it update *automatically*. **Core Concepts:** * **Signals:** The "atoms" of state. * **Fin
a: Well the API is an almost perfect replica of SolidJs, except for needing hyperscript functions instead of TSX/JSX. The issue is that the experience editor will not accept TSX unless it's entirely encapsulated as a string. The other option would be to have to write a transpiler to convert the TSX into TS. The second issue is that it would be a bit more complicated to write a parser for the TSX-style markup to be processed in the first place. I wanted something a bit quicker that would allow for custom functional components that anybody can build, like clocks, progress bars, toggles, drop-downs,

For what it's worth, not everything justifies a reactive UI as opposed to just using my UI class and calling setters whenever you need. For example, my `Logger` module actually runs worse with a reactive UI because of how many elements there are on screen that need to all be shifted upwards when a new line comes in. If each upward shift is a micro task, it's slower than just handling all those shifts in a for-loop. So to properly take advantage of SolidUI in Logger, I would need to refactor the way certain things work to reduce the amount of micro tasks by doing some effects in bulk, or maybe
entries.tt: SolidUI: A Reactive UI Framework for Portal

Now, you can pass an option to for each and any `SolidUI` managed component with `deferredTicks`, which will coalesce all updates due to signal changes that each respective property is listening to, and only actually update the UI widget property after the n

entries.q: why do you need to use mod.Equals to compare mod.Team types? Cause youre comparing the pointer? Can you override operators in ts? what do people usually do for this, just use mod.Equals?
a: The SDK has all their objects as opaque Symbols because they are just "references" to actual objects in their C++ code for the game engine. So for example, every time you `GetTeam` for a player, you get a completely unique Js object even if under the hood it references the same team. The only way to compare them is to either use `Equals` which does a comparison under the hood, or `GetObjId` to get the primitive `number` which then can be compared.

entries.q: What if the events are custom and dont exist in the api?
a: Then you build a class that allows other code to subscribe to and/or trigger those events.

If something in the game is causing you to change the state such that it would "trigger your custom event", then that same process should alert all subscribers (or call their callbacks) at that moment. You need to make sure that you allow for those callbacks to be either synchronous or asynchronous: The trade-offs are that synchronous callbacks will block all other execution, whereas asynchronous callbacks, if done correctly, will be individually put onto the micro task queue and handle individually without blocking the thing that caused the event

a: This is going to be a tough one because technically it's not a bug since on the kill feed suicides do show up as self kills and they got to be tracked somewhere. And the person responsible for that kill is in fact the person themselves, which is why the event gets triggered where that player is both the killer and the victim. I think the fact that there is a trivial workaround is sufficient to keep the current implementation of the API. But that's just my opinion.

I understand that it is technically a "kill" because the player killed themselves, but in the scoreboard, it isn't displayed as an actual kill. If `GetPlayerKills` doesn't reflect real kills made specifically against other players, I don't see it being very useful for most game logic. Since the default scoreboard only counts kills against other players, the game must not be using `GetPlayerKills` internally to set that value. If changing the logic of that specific method is too complicated, it would be great if they could add a separate method that excludes suicides. This would prevent us from

entries.q: So the issue is actually in `resolveImport`. When you go into the loop where you check against `extensions`, if the resolved file is `/index.ts` you append that to the path and return it. The issue is when you append it you always append it with `/`. To fix it you can just call `path.normalize(appended)` and return that instead. It will then always use the correct paths for the current OS.
a: Or just `path.join(targetPath, ext)` in the first place instead of manually appending
Ah, true. I'll include that in the fix
Directly using `path.join` won't work, turns out I just broke other things. `path.normalize` does seem to work

entries.q: Hi Everyone, I have created a layer on top of `bf6-portal-utils` toolkit which can be a solid starting point for anyone who would like to create portal mods of any size using TypeScript. Why use this template? - Solid starting feature set: included familiar UI elements, handling of capture points, team/player state, and a scoreboard. - Grows with your mod: object-oriented structure that stays readable as your project expands. - Easy to extend: clear separation of concerns and event-driven modules. - Reusable UI layer: UI is driven by accessors/signals instead of being hard-wired to game logic.
a: What's really cool is that `SolidUI` doesn't actually care what the underlying "interface" library is, so if we build a spatial object library, you can control in world spatial objects via game state signals the same way you can for UI.

Uses grid hashing. Effectively, some cheap function that converts a player's position into an id. It's a trade-off between computation and specificity.

It depends on the implementation. You can have a global or per player update frequency (maybe it even takes into account the fastest you know player can move). Then you can just choose to use the ID directly to know what specific cubic volume they are in, but it won't obviously give you the distance to a specific point. However, you can quickly compute the grid hash ID of the point you care about, and then filter for players in that grid hash, and then only check their distance.
he does a comparison at the end of the naive solution vs gridhash. But you really get bigger gains when you have more nodes.

entries.q: When you deploy as human, it should say in the error log that you deployed. When you deploy to a vehicle, it should say in the error log that you deployed to a vehicle. It should also say that you entered a vehicle from deployment. When you enter a vehicle, it should say in the error log that you entered a vehicle. When you get kicked out of a vehicle and teleported back to your HQ, it should reset your vehicle deploy variable so that you can still enter a vehicle and not get stuck in that loop since you are well past deployment at that point.
a: If you get the correct error messages about the player deploying to a vehicle, but they don't seem to enforce the action properly, try increasing the first wait time in rule #7 to more than 0.5 seconds. It needs to know that they deployed to a vehicle before it does that check.
